notes.meaning: God gives special instructions for the guilt offering, calling it most holy. This means the animal was set apart entirely for sacred use, dedicated either to God on the altar or given to the priests. Unlike common meals, ordinary worshipers could not eat any part of it.

The animal was killed at the north side of the altar, just like the regular burnt offering. The priest then splashed its blood against all four sides of the altar. This showed that the penalty of death was paid to restore the broken boundary caused by sin.

The priest removed the best parts of the animal, including the fat tail, the fat around the internal organs, the kidneys, and part of the liver. All of this rich fat was burned on the altar as a gift by fire to the Lord. God claimed the richest portions for Himself before anyone else received a share.

The meat that remained was given to the male members of the priest's family to eat. Because the sacrifice was most holy, they had to eat it within the sacred courtyard of the tabernacle. God made sure the priests who served Him were fed from the gifts brought to His altar.

The rules for dividing the guilt offering were the same as those for the sin offering. After the blood and fat were given to God, the meat belonged to the specific priest who performed the sacrifice. Atonement means repairing the damage of sin to make peace with God, and God rewarded the priest who did this holy work.

When an animal was offered as a burnt offering, all its meat was completely burned up on the altar. The officiating priest, however, was permitted to keep the animal's hide for himself. This provided clothing or leather goods as part of God's daily care for His workers.

Grain offerings cooked in ovens, pans, or griddles were given directly to the priest who offered them, since cooked food spoiled quickly. Uncooked grain offerings, whether dry or mixed with oil, were divided equally among all the priests on duty. God established fair rules so that both the priest doing the physical labor and those assisting him received their daily bread.

God introduces the rules for the peace offering, which was brought to celebrate fellowship with Him. Unlike offerings for sin, this was a voluntary meal where God, the priest, and the worshiper shared parts of the sacrifice. It was an expression of joy and thankfulness for God's blessings.

If someone brought a peace offering to thank God for a special deliverance, they brought breads made with fine flour and olive oil. These included thick cakes mixed with oil, thin wafers coated with oil, and fried cakes. These breads accompanied the meat to make a full, rich thanksgiving feast.

Along with the unleavened cakes, the worshiper brought regular leavened bread to the thanksgiving meal. One loaf of each kind of bread was lifted up as a special gift to the Lord and then handed to the officiating priest. While leaven could never be burned on the altar, it was welcomed at the fellowship table where God's people feasted.

All the meat from a thanksgiving offering had to be eaten on the very day it was sacrificed. Nothing was allowed to remain until the next morning. God wanted His people to express their gratitude promptly and to share their food freely with others rather than hoarding it.

If a peace offering was brought to fulfill a personal vow or as a freewill gift, the family could eat the meat over two days. Any meat left over on the third day had to be burned in the fire. This rule kept the sacred meat from spoiling in the warm climate and protected the holy feast from neglect.

Eating any leftover meat on the third day made the entire sacrifice worthless in God's eyes. Instead of receiving God's favor, the person who ate it committed a serious offense and bore the guilt of profaning holy food. A worshiper could not turn a sacred feast into an ordinary meal by disobeying God's timetable.

If sacrificial meat touched anything ceremonially unclean, it could not be eaten and had to be burned. Meat that remained pure could be shared by anyone who was clean according to God's law. God required His people to treat holy things with deep reverence and care.

Anyone who was ceremonially defiled—whether from sickness, a dead body, or an unclean animal—was strictly forbidden from eating sacred peace offering meat. If someone knowingly broke this command, they were cut off, meaning expelled from the community of Israel. Coming into God's presence while clinging to defilement showed open contempt for His holiness.

God tells Moses to instruct the people that they must never eat the fat of cattle, sheep, or goats. These were the domestic animals used for sacrifices on God's altar. Because the richest fat was reserved for the Lord alone, the people had to treat it as holy.

If an animal died naturally or was torn apart by wild predators, its fat could still be used for practical purposes like greasing tools, but no one could eat it. Eating the fat of an animal that could be offered to God was strictly forbidden. Anyone who ate this fat was cut off, meaning expelled from the community for taking what belonged to God.

God strictly forbade eating blood from any bird or land animal, anywhere the Israelites lived. Anyone who consumed blood was cut off from the nation. God reserved blood for Himself because it represented the life of the animal and was chosen to make atonement for human sin.

The worshiper who brought a peace offering had to present God's portion with his own hands rather than sending someone else. He brought the fat to be burned, along with the animal's breast to be moved back and forth before the Lord as a wave offering. This action showed that the giver was personally and gladly dedicating the gift to the Master of all the earth.

The priest burned the fat upon the altar fire as the Lord's share. The breast, after being waved before God, was given to Aaron and his sons for their food. God received His tribute first and then fed His ministers from the very gifts brought to Him.

The right thigh of the peace offering was lifted up as a contribution and given specifically to the priest who conducted the service. God took the wave breast for all the priests and the right thigh for the officiating priest as their permanent right from Israel. When God's people gave to the Lord, He made sure those who led worship were faithfully supported.

These food portions were assigned to Aaron and his sons on the day Moses anointed them to serve as priests. God established this as an everlasting law throughout all generations in Israel. Those who give their lives to spiritual service can trust God's enduring promise to supply their needs.

These verses wrap up the instructions for all the major sacrifices: the burnt, grain, sin, guilt, ordination, and peace offerings. The Lord delivered these complete commands to Moses at Mount Sinai while Israel was encamped in the wilderness. God left nothing to human guesswork, showing that true worship follows His exact word.
